title: Move the cafe to the cloud
facts: The cafe runs one shop today and plans 12 shops within 2 years, one of them abroad where customer data must stay in that country.
Online orders climb to 10 times the usual rate between 07:00 and 09:00 each morning.
A loyalty app lets regulars collect stamps and order ahead from their phones.
The cafe keeps 2 TB of receipts and product photos and must hold them for 7 years.
A point-of-sale server in the back office of the first shop records every sale.
One part-time IT person looks after every system the cafe runs.
The whole cloud bill must stay under a cap of $300 per month.

decisions.title: Deployment model and shared responsibility
decisions.prompt: Choose a deployment model for the cafe, name the 3 cloud benefits that matter most to it, and say where the shared responsibility line falls.
context: The cafe runs one shop today and plans 12 shops within 2 years.
One part-time IT person looks after every system, so less hands-on upkeep matters.
The whole cloud bill must stay under a cap of $300 per month.

keyPoints.text: The cafe picks a cloud-based deployment, since it has no regulated system that must stay in-house, so it starts small without buying servers and keeps hybrid only as a short bridge for the back-office till.

read.text: It scales well with little upfront cost, but alone cannot keep sensitive data on premises for compliance.

keyPoints.text: Trading fixed for variable expense matters because the cafe pays only for what each shop uses each month, which keeps the bill small enough to stay inside its monthly budget cap.

read.text: On AWS the bill follows monthly usage, so you start small, spending matches consumption for more financial flexibility, and billing and budgeting tools help you save.

keyPoints.text: Stopping the guesswork on capacity matters because the cafe can size for its single shop now and add resources as each new shop opens, rather than buying hardware for a growth forecast.

read.text: On AWS you provision for today and scale with real demand in minutes, not weeks or months, keeping performance optimal without over- or under-provisioning.

keyPoints.text: Leaving the running of data centers to AWS matters because the lone part-time IT person no longer racks, powers or repairs hardware and can spend those hours on the cafe's own systems.

read.text: AWS runs that physical layer, freeing time and money for customers and strategy.

keyPoints.text: The line falls where AWS secures the buildings, hardware and hypervisor, while the cafe still patches any operating system it runs and controls its own data, apps and who can reach them.

read.text: AWS owns security of the cloud, including all physical security, and the customer owns security in the cloud.

decisions.title: Compute for online ordering
decisions.prompt: Pick the compute for online ordering, covering the instance family, the purchase option, scaling, load balancing and queueing.
context: Online orders climb to 10 times the usual rate between 07:00 and 09:00 each morning.
An order that arrives during the morning rush must never be lost.
The whole cloud bill must stay under a cap of $300 per month.

keyPoints.text: The ordering web servers run on a small general purpose instance, since a balanced mix suits a web front end with unpredictable load, and a modest size keeps each server cheap under the monthly cap.

read.text: Unknown workload: start with general purpose.

keyPoints.text: A Savings Plan covers the few servers that run all day, the extra servers for the morning rush run On-Demand, and Spot is ruled out because AWS could reclaim a server while it holds orders.

read.text: Match the model to the usage: unknown means On-Demand, steady means Savings Plans or RIs, and interruptible but never critical means Spot.

keyPoints.text: An Auto Scaling group adds ordering servers as the breakfast surge builds, can schedule them ahead of that daily peak, and removes them afterwards, so the cafe pays for rush capacity only while the rush lasts.

read.text: Auto Scaling uses CloudWatch metrics to add and remove instances, dynamically or predictively.

keyPoints.text: A managed load balancer gives customers one address for ordering and spreads their requests over however many servers Auto Scaling is running, so no single server gets swamped at breakfast.

read.text: In front of an Auto Scaling group it is the single entry point, spreading requests evenly over whatever instances exist.

keyPoints.text: Each order goes into an Amazon SQS queue between the order website and the order processing servers, so a burst waits safely in line and no order is lost when the processors are busy or down.

read.text: It moves any volume of messages between components without losing them, and the receiver need not be available at send time.

decisions.title: Serverless and containers
decisions.prompt: Decide which parts of the cafe's software become serverless or run in containers, and explain why.
context: The loyalty app and online ordering see short, sharp bursts of use.
One part-time IT person has little time to patch and update servers.

keyPoints.text: The loyalty app and order-ahead requests run as Lambda functions fired by each request, so capacity grows for the sharp bursts and shrinks again when the shop is quiet.

read.text: It is highly available and scales up or down by itself, from one trigger to thousands.

keyPoints.text: Because Lambda bills only for the compute time code actually uses, the idle hours between bursts cost the cafe next to nothing, which keeps the monthly bill under its cap.

read.text: You pay per millisecond of compute, priced by memory.

keyPoints.text: Choosing serverless over self-run EC2 servers hands patching, scaling and availability to AWS, so the part-time IT person only looks after the app code and keeping it safe.

read.text: What stays with you under Lambda is the application code and keeping it secure.

keyPoints.text: Any part the cafe ships as a container, such as the ordering service, runs on Amazon ECS with Fargate, so AWS runs the hosts and the cafe pays only for what the containers use.

read.text: Fargate: serverless, so AWS runs the servers while ECS or EKS orchestrates, and you pay only for resources used.

keyPoints.text: Long jobs such as building the end-of-day sales report stay out of Lambda unless they split into short pieces, since each function run is capped at 15 minutes.

read.text: A run lasts 15 minutes at most, so work that cannot be split into such chunks may fit elsewhere.

decisions.title: Regions, edge and repeatable infrastructure
decisions.prompt: Choose a Region for the shop abroad, a way to deliver content from the edge, and a way to build the same infrastructure again for each new shop.
context: One of the 12 planned shops is abroad, and its customer data must stay in that country.
Customers open the loyalty app wherever they happen to be.
Each new shop should get the same setup without manual steps.

keyPoints.text: The shop abroad runs in a Region inside its own country, because the local rule that its customer data stays at home decides the choice before nearness, features or price are weighed.

read.text: Check compliance first, since a legal rule can settle the Region alone, but most businesses have none and move on to the rest.

keyPoints.text: Before committing to the in-country Region for the shop abroad, the cafe confirms that the services its ordering and loyalty systems need are offered there and budgets for that Region's own prices, so the monthly cap still holds.

read.text: Regions are isolated, follow local law, and differ in services and prices.

keyPoints.text: Menu images and app content go out through CloudFront from edge locations near each customer, so the loyalty app stays quick wherever it is opened without extra servers in every country.

read.text: Amazon CloudFront, a content delivery network (CDN) and cache, uses them to serve images, video, apps and APIs near users.

keyPoints.text: Each new shop's setup is launched from one shared CloudFormation template, so every shop gets identical resources from a single command and the IT person avoids slips from repeated manual steps.

read.text: One template across accounts or Regions gives identical environments from one command, with fewer errors and more resilience.

keyPoints.text: Keeping the infrastructure as code under version control beats clicking through the console or growing ad hoc scripts, which drift apart and grow hard to maintain as the shop count rises.

read.text: For consistent multi-Region rollouts, the console fits only small one-off jobs, scripts automate partly but get hard to maintain, and mixing methods causes drift.

decisions.title: Network layout and shop connections
decisions.prompt: Lay out the virtual network, set the stance for security groups and network access control lists, and choose how the shops connect to it.
context: The point-of-sale server in the back office must reach the cloud safely.
The cafe will grow from one shop to 12 shops within 2 years.
The ordering servers face the internet while the databases must not.

keyPoints.text: The cafe's VPC holds the ordering servers in public subnets whose route table points at an internet gateway, and the databases in private subnets with no such route, so customers reach the ordering site but never the databases.

read.text: A subnet only becomes public when its associated route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 traffic to an attached internet gateway.

keyPoints.text: Security groups let only HTTPS into the ordering servers and only ordering server traffic into the databases, and because they are stateful the replies flow back without extra rules.

read.text: You open it with allow rules, such as accepting only HTTPS on a web server, with separate inbound and outbound rules, and anything not allowed stays blocked.

keyPoints.text: A custom network ACL guards the private subnets as a second, subnet-wide layer that blocks everything the cafe has not allowed, with rules for both directions since it remembers nothing, and the cafe owns writing these rules.

read.text: A custom network ACL starts the other way round: nothing passes until you add allow rules.

keyPoints.text: The back office point-of-sale server reaches the VPC through an encrypted Site-to-Site VPN into a virtual private gateway, since a few sales records need no dedicated Direct Connect line and its extra bandwidth.

read.text: Choose it only when you need the bandwidth, since plain site links suit Site-to-Site VPN.

keyPoints.text: As the cafe opens more shops, a transit gateway acts as one hub that each shop link and VPC joins, instead of a tangle of separate connections, and it can peer with the shop abroad's Region.

read.text: AWS Transit Gateway: a central hub for VPCs and on-premises networks, with inter-Region peering between transit gateways.

decisions.title: Storage classes and lifecycle
decisions.prompt: Choose storage classes and lifecycle rules for receipts, product images and point-of-sale backups.
context: The cafe keeps 2 TB of receipts and product photos and must hold them for 7 years.
Old receipts are rarely opened once a year has passed.
The whole cloud bill must stay under a cap of $300 per month.

keyPoints.text: Product photos that the menu site and loyalty app show all day sit in S3 Standard, because they are read constantly and must load fast for every customer.

read.text: S3 Standard: the general-purpose default when no class is named, with fast retrieval at an affordable price, for apps, games, dynamic websites, content distribution and big data analytics.

keyPoints.text: A lifecycle rule moves each receipt to a cheaper class as it ages, so fresh receipts stay quick to open while old ones stop paying the frequent-access rate, with no manual copying.

read.text: Transition actions move objects to another class at a set age, such as Standard-IA after 30 days or Glacier Deep Archive after a year.

keyPoints.text: Receipts nobody opens after their first year end up in S3 Glacier Deep Archive, the cheapest class, since a slow restore is fine for a compliance record checked once in a while.

read.text: Meant for long-term retention and digital preservation, such as compliance archives that finance, healthcare or government keep 7-10 years or more.

keyPoints.text: An expiration action deletes each receipt once its legal holding period ends, so the archive reaches back no further than the law requires and the cafe stops paying to store records it no longer must keep.

read.text: Expiration actions delete objects for good, such as when compliance no longer needs them.

keyPoints.text: Point-of-sale backups go to S3 Standard-IA, which stores them cheaply while they sit unused yet returns them fast on the bad day a restore is needed, at the cost of a retrieval fee.

read.text: S3 Standard-IA: data used less often but needed fast, with S3 Standard's durability, throughput and latency, cheaper storage and a per-GiB retrieval fee, for backups and disaster recovery files.

decisions.title: Databases and caching
decisions.prompt: Pick a database for each workload of the cafe and decide where caching helps.
context: Every sale from the point-of-sale server needs a reliable record.
The loyalty app reads the same menu and stamp balances many times each morning.
Online orders climb to 10 times the usual rate between 07:00 and 09:00.

keyPoints.text: Point-of-sale records go into Amazon RDS, a managed relational database, because each sale is structured transactional data that must stay consistent while AWS handles the patching and backups the part-time IT person has no time for.

read.text: A relational service for operational workloads, not data warehousing, that automates patching, backups, provisioning, failover and disaster recovery.

keyPoints.text: The sales database runs as a Multi-AZ deployment with automated backups, so a standby in a second Availability Zone takes over if the primary fails and no recorded sale is lost.

read.text: Resilience: Multi-AZ, automated backups on your schedule, and manual DB snapshots (full copies for point-in-time recovery or archives).

keyPoints.text: Loyalty profiles and stamp balances live in Amazon DynamoDB, whose flexible schema lets one regular store a favorite drink and another a birthday, with no servers for the cafe to maintain.

read.text: Fully managed, serverless NoSQL for key-value and document data.

keyPoints.text: DynamoDB auto scaling raises table throughput for the morning order surge and lowers it again once the rush ends, so orders stay fast at the peak without paying for peak capacity all day.

read.text: Auto scaling with provisioned capacity: throughput automatically follows real use toward your target utilization, steady at peaks, cheaper when quiet.

keyPoints.text: An Amazon ElastiCache layer answers the repeated morning reads of the menu and popular lookups from memory, which takes load off the database and can let the cafe run a smaller, cheaper instance under its budget.

read.text: Reading from the cache can let you run smaller, cheaper database instances.

decisions.title: Analytics and an AI feature
decisions.prompt: Design one analytics pipeline over the cafe's sales and add one AI feature that helps customers or staff.
context: Sales from every shop and from the loyalty app pile up each day.
The owners want to know which items sell at which hour.
One part-time IT person cannot run a large data platform.

keyPoints.text: Sales from every shop's till and from the loyalty app are gathered into one S3 data lake, so the owners analyze a single shared copy instead of chasing figures spread over separate systems.

read.text: Purchases, logins and browsing leave data scattered across systems and formats, and a data lake, pictured as a huge reservoir, gathers it all.

keyPoints.text: The ingest step uses Amazon Data Firehose, a managed service that takes in each day's sales and delivers them in near real time, so the one part-time IT person has no ingestion system of their own to run.

read.text: Amazon Data Firehose: Managed near-real-time ingestion and delivery.

keyPoints.text: The AWS Glue Data Catalog records the layout of the sales files, so Amazon Athena can answer which items sell at which hour with plain SQL run on the lake in place, with no warehouse to build or look after.

read.text: 7 Perform data analytics: data scientists query S3 in place with standard SQL in Amazon Athena, which reads the catalog table to recognize the structure.

keyPoints.text: Amazon Quick Sight shows the owners a dashboard of item sales by hour that they open themselves, which suits business reporting better than a search and monitoring tool.

read.text: QuickSight is for BI dashboards, while OpenSearch Service is for real-time search and monitoring.

keyPoints.text: The AI feature is Amazon Personalize showing each loyalty app regular a personalized drink recommendation, which helps customers pick their order in the app.

read.text: Amazon Personalize: Personalized recommendations.

decisions.title: Identity, encryption and edge protection
decisions.prompt: Set up identities and root user protection, choose how data is encrypted, and protect the ordering site at the edge.
context: The part-time IT person and every shop manager need some access, but not the same access.
Receipts and loyalty records hold customer details.
The ordering site faces the internet during the morning rush.

keyPoints.text: The owner's root user gets a strong password and MFA on day one and is then kept out of everyday jobs, since nothing can limit what it does in the cafe's account.

read.text: Give it a strong password and turn on multi-factor authentication (MFA) right after the first root login.

keyPoints.text: The IT person and each shop manager sign in with their own identity in a group for their job, and each group's policy allows only that job's tasks, so a manager cannot touch the network or billing.

read.text: Least privilege is the guiding principle: allow only what a person or system needs.

keyPoints.text: Receipts and loyalty records stay encrypted at rest under keys held in AWS KMS, and the cafe chooses which roles may use those keys, so a stolen copy of customer details cannot be read.

read.text: You set which IAM users and roles may manage keys and where they are used, keys never leave KMS, and a key can be disabled temporarily.

keyPoints.text: The ordering site and loyalty app accept only HTTPS, using TLS certificates that ACM manages, so names, orders and stamp balances are encrypted on the way between phones and the cafe.

read.text: SSL and its successor TLS use certificates to verify identity, then encrypt the connection.

keyPoints.text: Customers reach the ordering site through a load balancer or CloudFront, where free Shield Standard soaks up common DDoS floods and AWS WAF rules turn away bad requests, so the morning rush still gets served.

read.text: AWS Shield Standard: free, automatic, real-time defense against common DDoS attacks, built into ELB, CloudFront and Route 53.

decisions.title: Monitoring, audit and governance
decisions.prompt: Choose how the cafe monitors its systems, keeps an audit trail, structures its accounts and gathers compliance evidence.
context: The part-time IT person must hear about a problem before customers do.
The shop abroad brings its own rules for customer data.
The cafe will run 12 shops within 2 years.

keyPoints.text: CloudWatch alarms on order errors and server load text the part-time IT person through Amazon SNS the moment a threshold is crossed, so a fault is caught before customers notice it.

read.text: An alarm can notify through SNS or scale EC2 automatically.

keyPoints.text: A CloudTrail trail delivers every API call to log files in Amazon S3, giving the cafe a lasting record of who changed what and when, well past the short free event history.

read.text: Event history is free for 90 days, while S3 logs serve long audits.

keyPoints.text: AWS Organizations gives each shop its own member account, grouped into OUs, and the shop abroad sits in an OU whose SCP caps the services its accounts may use under local data rules.

read.text: Base OUs on each department's business, security and regulatory needs.

keyPoints.text: AWS Config rules keep checking each shop's resources against the cafe's settings and flag or fix any that drift, so new shops stay compliant without the IT person inspecting them by hand.

read.text: It alerts you to noncompliant resources and can fix them automatically.

keyPoints.text: AWS Audit Manager gathers proof of the cafe's controls on its own, and AWS Artifact Reports supply AWS's audits, so the regulator abroad gets ready evidence instead of a hand-built pile.

read.text: Audit Manager is fully managed, audits usage continually and automates evidence collection across teams.

decisions.title: Cost, budgets and Support plan
decisions.prompt: Estimate the monthly cost, set budgets and alerts, and pick a Support plan by its current name.
context: The whole cloud bill must stay under a cap of $300 per month.
The part-time IT person needs help quickly when something breaks.
Spending grows each time the cafe opens a new shop.

keyPoints.text: Before anything is deployed, the cafe enters its chosen instances, storage and expected traffic into the AWS Pricing Calculator, so it can check the monthly estimate against its cap and compare cheaper designs first.

read.text: The Pricing Calculator estimates costs before deployment.

keyPoints.text: The monthly estimate prices compute, storage and outbound data transfer, the three main cost drivers, so the cafe's cloud compute instances, the product photos it stores in the cloud and the data sent out to customers are all counted against the cap.

read.text: The three main drivers are compute, storage and outbound data transfer.

keyPoints.text: An AWS Budgets budget set below the monthly cap warns the part-time IT person as spend nears or passes the limit, since Cost Explorer can forecast spend but never sends that alert.

read.text: Budgets and Cost Explorer both forecast, but only Budgets sends threshold alerts.

keyPoints.text: Every resource carries a shop tag that is activated for cost allocation, so Cost Explorer shows which new shop pushed the bill up and the cafe can adjust before the next opening.

read.text: Cost Explorer can allocate costs by tags such as project, department or environment, showing who drives spend.

keyPoints.text: The cafe picks AWS Business Support+ for its live ordering system, giving the lone IT person fast technical cases when something breaks, rather than a higher plan whose extras, such as a designated technical account manager, a small cafe does not need.

read.text: AWS calls Business Support+ the minimum plan it recommends for production workloads.

decisions.title: Migration strategies and data transfer
decisions.prompt: Choose a migration strategy for each existing system and a method to move the cafe's data.
context: The point-of-sale server in the back office holds every sale so far.
The cafe keeps 2 TB of receipts and product photos.
The shops cannot close for long while their systems move.

keyPoints.text: Each existing system gets its own migration path rather than one rule for everything, so the cafe moves each piece the cheapest safe way and keeps disruption to the shops low.

read.text: Organizations often combine them into a tailored plan with less risk and disruption.

keyPoints.text: The sales database behind the point-of-sale server is replatformed onto Amazon RDS with no code changes, so the part-time IT person stops patching the database engine by hand.

read.text: MySQL to Amazon RDS with no code changes: replatform.

keyPoints.text: AWS DMS copies the sales history while the point-of-sale database keeps taking orders, so the shops only pause for a short switch-over instead of closing for the whole move.

read.text: You name the source and target, and a scheduled task on a replication VM copies the data while the source stays live.

keyPoints.text: The receipts and product photos travel online into Amazon S3 with AWS DataSync, scheduled and throttled outside opening hours so the copy never slows the shop's own connection.

read.text: It handles instances, encryption and network tuning, and lets you throttle, schedule, filter and report on tasks.

keyPoints.text: Shipping a Snow Family device is not worth it for the cafe, because its archive is far below petabyte scale and the shop has a working internet link to send it over.

read.text: Triggers: thin bandwidth, remote sites without internet or Direct Connect, or petabytes that ship faster than they upload.

decisions.title: Well-Architected review
decisions.prompt: Review the whole design against the six Well-Architected pillars and name the top 3 fixes.
context: The earlier decisions now describe the cafe's whole design.
One part-time IT person must be able to run what the plan builds.
The whole cloud bill must stay under a cap of $300 per month.

keyPoints.text: The cafe reviews its whole design in the free, self-service AWS Well-Architected Tool, checking it against all six pillars without adding anything to the capped monthly bill.

read.text: A free, self-service AWS service for reviewing and improving workloads against the six pillars.

keyPoints.text: A top fix for operational excellence is shipping changes through AWS CodePipeline instead of by hand, so the lone part-time IT person avoids the outages and drifting setups that hand-run releases can cause.

read.text: Hand-run releases causing outages and drifting environments: a CI/CD pipeline such as AWS CodePipeline (Operational Excellence).

keyPoints.text: Under the security pillar, the review checks that staff and services get only the permissions they need and that loyalty and order data stay encrypted, closing gaps a busy IT person could miss.

read.text: Pillar cues: automated releases point to Operational Excellence, least privilege and encryption to Security, multiple AZs and recovery to Reliability.

keyPoints.text: The reliability check asks how ordering recovers when a server or zone fails mid-rush, so the cafe keeps orders flowing across zones with automated recovery as it adds shops.

read.text: Reliability: planning recovery from failures and adapting as business and customer needs grow.

keyPoints.text: Rightsizing underused servers, choosing cheaper purchase options and preferring serverless over always-on machines serve performance, cost and sustainability together and keep the bill under its cap.

read.text: Fitting size to workload points to Performance Efficiency, purchase options and deprovisioning to Cost Optimization, serverless over always-on to Sustainability.
